criterion_notes.c1: Examines household domestic water service access and water security in Pinget, Baguio City, Philippines, including municipal utility metered connections (Baguio Water District, BWD), shared connections, tank/truck delivery, consumption, ease of access, cleanliness, and affordability.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, though borderline in quantitative framing. Under the plain wording, the study clearly examines institutional/governance and tenure factors related to municipal utility (BWD) water access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, while the quantitative regressions conceptualize BWD connection status and homeownership as household physical resources rather than isolating a legal rule, the primary qualitative empirical component (Aim 2, n = 18 interviews plus BWD personnel inquiry, pp. 505-506) directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing access to a BWD household connection: (1) tariff/cost-recovery rules (PHP 6,000 connection fee plus homeowner responsibility for PHP 4,000-8,000 in meter-to-home piping), (2) discretion/accommodation rules (an installment payment plan requiring PHP 3,000 down and PHP 3,000 over 3 months, granted on a case-by-case basis with low public awareness), and (3) administrative burden and informal rent-seeking in application processing (needing to regularly follow up and 'be annoyingly persistent,' plus reported 'under the table' payments). Per the qualitative socio-legal safeguard, these empirical mechanism findings support inclusion.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical evidence: a stratified random survey of N = 396 households analyzed using multiple imputation and linear/logistic regressions, combined with n = 18 purposively sampled in-depth interviews coded in NVIVO 9.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports four quantitative household water access/security outcomes—reported water consumption (liters per capita per day), perceived cleanliness, perceived ease of obtaining water, and affordability (water expenditures as a share of household income)—as well as household BWD connection status and qualitative exclusion/barriers to obtaining a utility connection.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (households / household water managers in Pinget, Baguio City; N = 396 surveys, n = 18 interviews), exposures/mechanisms (household financial, physical, and social resources including tenure/homeownership and BWD connection status, plus qualitative BWD connection fee, discretionary installment, and application burden mechanisms), outcomes, and cross-sectional mixed-methods study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English (surveys and interviews were conducted in local languages with multilingual research assistants and reported in English).

evidence_quotes.quote: About one quarter (25.8%) of households reported no access to a BWD connection, 31.1% reported shared access (e.g., through a neighbor or relative), and 43.2% reported having their own household connection to the utility.

To obtain a BWD connection, households must pay the ₱6,000 connection fee. In addition, the homeowner must bear an estimated ₱4,000 to ₱8,000 in additional costs for installing pipes from the BWD meter to the home. This combined cost of ₱10,000 to ₱14,000 ($234 to $327) is prohibitive for many households.
however, this option is available on a case-by-case basis only. Further, awareness of the installment payment option appears to be limited among Pinget households.

A consistent theme among participants’ comments regarding the BWD connection process was the need to regularly follow up with BWD about an application, or, as one participant said, “be annoyingly persistent.”
Among the sample of 416 eligible units, 95.2% participated in the study (N = 396).
Dependent variables included reported consumption, perceived cleanliness, perceived ease, and affordability.

raw_response.exposure: Quantitative: household financial resources (monthly income, savings), physical resources (tank/drum storage capacity, Baguio Water District [BWD] metered connection status, homeownership status), and social borrowing networks. Qualitative: BWD connection fee and pipe cost rules (PHP 6,000 fee plus PHP 4,000-8,000 piping), discretionary case-by-case connection fee installment plan rules (PHP 3,000 down plus PHP 3,000 over 3 months), and administrative burden/informal payment barriers in BWD application processing.
raw_response.outcome: Quantitative: reported dry-season water consumption (liters per capita per day), perceived cleanliness (PCA score), perceived ease of obtaining water, and affordability (monthly water expenses <=10% vs >10% of household income). Qualitative: attainment of a household BWD metered connection and household water security coping.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households (self-identified household water managers) in Pinget neighborhood, Baguio City, Philippines; stratified random sample of N = 396 household surveys (out of 1,793 housing units) and purposive sample of n = 18 in-depth interviews.
raw_response.rationale: This mixed-methods empirical study in urban Baguio City, Philippines (N = 396 household surveys; n = 18 in-depth interviews) examines household water service access, consumption, perceived cleanliness, ease of access, and affordability. Although the quantitative regression models focus primarily on household financial, physical, and social resources (modeling homeownership and BWD utility connection status as physical resources), Aim 2's qualitative empirical analysis directly investigates rule-type utility mechanisms governing access to a BWD municipal connection—specifically upfront connection fees and piping cost-allocation rules (PHP 6,000 + PHP 4,000-8,000), a strict installment payment plan granted only on a discretionary case-by-case basis with low household awareness, and administrative burdens/informal payment pressures during application follow-up. Under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (together with the safeguard retaining empirical qualitative mechanism evidence), the study meets all inclusion criteria.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods study (stratified random household survey analyzed via multiple imputation and linear/logistic regression, paired with purposive in-depth qualitative interviews)
